name: Egyptian Ful Medames
description: Ful medames, slow-simmered fava beans mashed with garlic, lemon, and olive oil, is widely considered Egypt's national dish, eaten most often for breakfast.
steps_detailed: Simmer the fava beans with a splash of water, 8-10 minutes, until very soft.
Mash roughly, leaving some texture, and stir in the garlic, lemon juice, cumin, and olive oil.

name: Egyptian Koshari
description: Koshari, layered rice, lentils, and pasta topped with a tangy tomato sauce and crispy fried onions, is Egypt's most beloved street food, with genuine roots reflecting Indian, Italian, and Middle Eastern culinary influence all in one dish.
steps_detailed: Cook the rice, lentils, and macaroni separately, each according to their own timing.
Fry the sliced onion in the oil over medium heat, stirring often, 12-15 minutes, until deeply crisp and browned - this crispy onion topping is essential to real koshari, not a garnish to skip.
Simmer the tomatoes with the garlic and vinegar, 10-12 minutes, into a tangy sauce.
Layer the rice, lentils, and macaroni in a bowl, top with the tomato sauce and crispy onions.

name: Egyptian Molokhia
description: Molokhia, a garlicky, mucilaginous green soup, is one of Egypt's most beloved comfort foods - real molokhia uses the leaves of a specific jute mallow plant, which isn't a distinct item here, so this uses spinach for a milder, less viscous approximation of the real texture.
steps_detailed: Finely chop the spinach.
Simmer the broth with the spinach 8-10 minutes.
Fry the garlic, cumin, and coriander in a little oil until fragrant, 30 seconds, then stir into the soup off the heat - this garlic tempering step is a real, essential part of molokhia's flavor.

name: Egyptian Ta'ameya
description: Ta'ameya, Egypt's fava-bean version of falafel, predates the more familiar chickpea-based falafel found elsewhere in the region and is coated in real sesame seeds before frying.
steps_detailed: Blend the fava beans, garlic, and cilantro into a coarse, thick paste.
Shape into small patties and press sesame seeds onto both sides.
Fry in the oil, turning, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply golden.

name: Egyptian Mahshi
description: Mahshi, vegetables stuffed with spiced rice, is a beloved Egyptian home-cooking dish, made in enormous batches for gatherings.
steps_detailed: Mix the raw rice with the cilantro and garlic.
Pack loosely into the hollowed zucchini, leaving room for the rice to expand.
Arrange in a pot, pour the tomatoes and 1 cup water over, cover, and simmer 30-35 minutes until the zucchini is tender.

name: Egyptian Shakshuka
description: Shakshuka, eggs poached in a spiced tomato sauce, shared across the wider Middle East and North Africa, a common Egyptian breakfast.
steps_detailed: Simmer the tomatoes, bell pepper, cumin, and garlic 10-12 minutes into a thick sauce.
Make small wells in the sauce and crack the eggs into them.
Cover and cook 5-6 minutes until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft.

name: Egyptian Dukkah
description: Dukkah, a toasted nut, seed, and spice blend, is a genuine Egyptian condiment, traditionally scooped up with bread dipped first in olive oil.
steps_detailed: Toast the hazelnuts, sesame seeds, coriander seed, and cumin separately in a dry pan until fragrant, watching closely so nothing burns.
Let cool, then coarsely grind together, keeping some texture rather than grinding to a powder.

name: Egyptian Feteer Meshaltet
description: Feteer meshaltet, a flaky, layered pastry, is a genuine Egyptian specialty, sometimes called Egyptian pancakes, served sweet or savory.
steps_detailed: Work the flour into a soft dough with water, then roll out very thin, brushing generously with melted butter between folds to build real flaky layers.
Fold and roll several times, then cook in a hot, dry pan, 3-4 minutes per side.
Drizzle with honey to serve.

Drizzle the honey over while still warm so it soaks in.
